n: Our....fellow-labourer, or coadjutor. He calls him so, because of the charity and zeal with which he promoted the gospel. (Witham)
And to the Church, or congregation of the faithful which is in thy house. (Witham)

Thy charity and faith....in the Lord Jesus,[1] and towards all the saints. In the Greek is towards Jesus Christ, and towards all the saints. By the saints he seems to mean, as elsewhere, all Christians; so that the sense may be, of thy faith towards Christ, and of thy charity towards all the saints or Christians. (Witham)

That the communication.[2] That is, charitable contributions, done with a lively faith, may become evident,[3] and the good works known, which are in you; that is, done among you. This seems the sense of the following verse, where St. Paul expresseth his joy in hearing of Philemon's charity towards the saints. (Witham)

Wherefore, though I might have much confidence, &c. Now St. Paul disposeth Philemon to grant his request, I am persuaded I might command thee, and thou wouldst not take it amiss. (Witham) --- To command thee, &c. As an apostle of Jesus Christ, I have the power even of ordering thee to forgive Onesimus, and to receive him again into favour; likewise as Paul, the aged, respect and regard being always due in a particular manner to old men; or again, as a prisoner of Jesus Christ, suffering here out of love for Jesus Christ and the faithful: I might here make use of all these different reasons to induce thee to pardon a poor fugitive slave, but I will not; I merely as a poor humble supplicant, forgetting all the dignity due to my apostleship, my grey hairs, or my chains, beseech thee to pardon him. Nor can I for a moment doubt of obtaining my request, when I consider the great charity thou hast in Jesus Christ towards all the saints. (Calmet; Haydock)

I rather beseech thee, thou being such a one,[4] as Paul. That is, united to him in spirit, by the same faith and charity; I am therefore confident thou wilt not refuse the request of Paul, now an aged man, and a prisoner, for the sake of Jesus Christ. (Witham)

I beseech thee, &c. He at length tells Philemon what his request is, and names the person Onesimus, but in such terms as shew how much St. Paul has this affair at heart, and that he will look upon the favour he asks as done to himself. It is, that thou wilt pardon Onesimus, whom I look upon and love as my son, and a most dear son, whom I have begotten, a prisoner, and in my chains. (Witham) --- How great is the ingenuity shewn by St. Paul in this epistle, in obtaining for Onesimus the pardon of his master, Philemon. Having in the preceding verse endeavoured by every argument which a real tenderness and compassion could inspire, and making use of every expression that could conciliate the favour of Philemon, to obtain his charitable request, he in this verse for the first time dares mention Onesimus by name; a name which he was sensible must sound harsh in the ears of one who had received an injury from him. See how he endeavours to prevent so unhappy an effect, by adding to the name every epithet that could any way tend to soften all feelings of asperity, and excite compassion and pity. I beseech thee then for my son, whom I have begotten, and that in my chains. (Calmet) --- The pardon I crave is not for your slave, but for my son. If in all antiquity there be any thing in the persuasive kind of eloquence truly admirable, it is this short epistle in which there are contained almost as many arguments as words.

Who heretofore was unprofitable to thee, in taking and spending what belonged to thee, yet now, after a sincere conversion, is profitable[5] both to me and thee; to me, by the services he has done me in prison; and the joy I have had by his conversion; and also to thee, because I know thou wouldst have been glad to have rendered me all possible services thyself, and he has done them for thee; he hath supplied thy place. For these reasons I could have wished to have detained him with me: but I have sent him back, thou being his master, nor would I do any thing in regard of thy servant, without thy advice and consent, that if thou thinkest it fitting to send him back again to me, and to give him his freedom, it may be without any constraint upon thee, without any necessity, thy voluntary and charitable act and deed. (Witham) --- St. Paul here makes an allusion to the word Onesimus, signifying useful in the Greek. He was before unprofitable, he says, to thee, contrary to the import of his name; but now he is truly an Onesimus, or useful, both to you and to me; to you indeed, by his conversion, and the resolution he now makes to serve you faithfully the remainder of his life; to me also, by the services he renders me in my chains. (Calmet) --- St. Jerome observes that some hypercritics pretended that this subject was not deserving the solicitude of an apostle, and on that account questioned its author; but this reasoning is unworthy of those who adore a God who did not refuse to die for rebellious and impious slaves. It shews pastors how solicitous they should always be for the salvation of the meanest of their flock; yes, though they may appear obdurate, and dead and buried in the pit of sin.

Do thou receive him as my own bowels. That is, as myself. Perhaps by the permission of God's providence (who never permits evil, but for some greater good) he departed from thee for a little while,[6] that thou mightest receive him for ever, being now after his conversion in a way of being made partaker with thee of the same eternal happiness. (Witham)

Receive him not now as a servant, but also as a most dear brother, especially to me. Nay I may say, how much more dear even to thee, both in the flesh, having been a Gentile as thou thyself wast, and having been also a servant in thy family. And secondly, he ought now to be dear to thee in our Lord, he who was thy servant, being now united to thee by the same faith, and by an union of charity. See Estius. (Witham)
If, therefore, thou count me a partner,[7] as a brother in Christ, as a member of Christ with thee, receive him as myself. (Witham)
If he hath wronged thee in any thing, as he confesses, put it to my account, to my debtor, I will repay it, and satisfy thee for it. (Witham)

I, Paul, have written, and testified this with my own hand. Some think he wrote the whole letter, with his own hand, to make it more acceptable to Philemon. --- Not to say to thee, that thou owest me thy own self, the eternal salvation of thy soul, by thy conversion to the faith of Christ. (Witham)

Yea, brother: may I enjoy thee in the Lord, enjoy the fruits of thy friendship and love for me, and rejoice with thee. In this refresh my bowels in the Lord, grant me this satisfaction. I have written freely, and with confidence in thy obedience; that is, ready compliance, in giving him and me more than I ask, to wit, his freedom. After this, he was made a deacon, and, as some say, a bishop and a martyr. See St. Jerome, and Tillemont in his art. 45. on St. Paul, and his notes 70, 71. (Witham) ____________________ [1] Ver. 5. Charitatem tuam et fidem, quam habes in Domino Jesu, et in omnes Sanctos; pros ton kurion Iesoun, kai eis pantas tous agious. [2] Ver. 6. Ut communicatio, e koinonia. See St. Paul, 1 Corinthians i. 9. &c. [3] Ver. 6. Evidens; most Greek copies, energes, efficax, but in some, enarges. [4] Ver. 9. Cum sis talis ut Paulus senex, toioutos on os Paulos presbutes. [5] Ver. 11. Onesimos, utilis, but he useth achrestos and euchrestos. See Cornelius a Lapide. [6] Ver. 15. A little while. Literally, ad horam, pros oran. [7] Ver. 17. As a partner, ut socium, koinonon.

f: Commentary on Philemon

In order to make the letter's authority from himself, he began by acknowledging his wrongdoing. Just as being bound is a disgrace because of sin, so on the contrary, for Christ to endure the chains of imprisonment is the greatest glory. For at the time he sent this letter, he was in custody. However, although Philemon was not a cleric, he nevertheless participated in the needs of the Church out of devotion, hence he says that he is a participant in these labors. For there are indeed many who, although worthy, excuse themselves, judging themselves unworthy of such a ministry; hence they appear truly worthy.
Commentary on Philemon

Philemon was not endowed with the dignity of ecclesiastical ordination, but he was an honorable man, one from the common people. For this reason, Onesimus, his servant and friend, writes him a letter; so that he may not only forgive him, but also give thanks to God; because he received him in such a way that he does not consider him a slave, but a most beloved brother.
Epistle 63

How many masters has he who has forsaken the One! But let us not forsake Him. Who would forsake Him Whom they follow bound with chains indeed, but chains of love, which set free and do not bind, those chains in which they who are bound boast, saying: "Paul the bondservant of Jesus Christ, and Timothy." It is more glorious for us to be bound by Him, than to be set free and loosed from others. Who then would flee from peace? Who would flee from salvation? Who would flee from mercy? Who would flee from redemption?
Homily Concerning the Statues 16

"Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ," saith he, "and Timothy the brother." Great is the designation of Paul: no title of principality and power, but he speaks of bonds and chains! Truly great indeed! Although many other things made him illustrious; his being caught up into the third heaven, his being transported to Paradise, his hearing unutterable words; yet he sets down none of these, but mentions the chain instead of all, for this made him more conspicuous and illustrious than these. And why so? Because the one were the free gifts of the Lord's lovingkindness; and the other the marks of the constancy and patience of the servant. But it is customary with those who love, to glory more in the things which they suffer for those who are beloved, than in the benefits they receive from them. A king is not so proud of his diadem, as Paul gloried in his chains. And very justly. For a diadem affords but an ornament to the crowned head; but the chain is a much greater ornament as well as a security.… But he, instead of all such titles, says, "Paul the prisoner." And very rightly. For those magisterial offices are no complete evidences of virtue in respect to the soul; for they are to be purchased by money, and obtained by the solicitations of friends; but this distinction that is obtained by bonds is a proof of the soul's love of wisdom, and the strongest sign of a longing for Christ.
Homily on Philemon 1

These things are said to a master in behalf of a servant. Immediately at the outset, he has pulled down his spirit, and not suffered him to be ashamed, he has quenched his anger; calling himself a prisoner, he strikes him with compunction, and makes him collect himself, and makes it appear that present things are nothing. For if a chain for Christ's sake is not a shame but a boast, much more is slavery not to be considered a reproach. And this he says, not exalting himself, but for a good purpose doing this, showing thence that he was worthy of credit; and this he does not for his own sake, but that he may more readily obtain the favor. As if he had said, "It is on your account that I am invested with this chain." As he also has said elsewhere, there indeed showing his concern, but here his trustworthiness.
Homily on Philemon 1

Nothing is greater than this boast, to be called "the stigmatized of Christ." "For I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus." (Gal. vi. 17.)

"The prisoner of the Lord." For he had been bound on His account. Who would not be struck with awe, who would not be humbled when he hears of the chains of Christ? Who would not be ready to give up even his own life, much less one domestic?
Homily on Philemon 1

"And Timothy our brother."

He joins another also with himself, that he, being entreated by many, may the more readily yield and grant the favor.
Homily on Philemon 1

"Unto Philemon our dearly beloved, and fellow-laborer."

If "beloved," then his confidence is not boldness nor forwardness, but a proof of much affection. If a "fellow-laborer," then not only may he be instructed in such a matter, but he ought to acknowledge it as a favor. For he is gratifying himself, he is building up the same work. So that apart from any request, he says, thou hast another necessity for granting the favor. For if he is profitable to the Gospel, and thou art anxious to promote the Gospel, then oughtest thou not to be entreated, but to entreat.
Commentary on Philemon

Those who refuse to receive among the Epistles of Paul the one which is written to Philemon say that the Apostle did not always, nor in all things, speak with Christ speaking in him. For, they argue, human weakness could not have borne the one unbroken course of the Holy Spirit; nor would the necessities of this poor body always be fulfilled in the presence of the Lord: such as arranging a meal, taking food, being hungry, being filled, digesting what has been taken in, replenishing what has been used up. I say nothing of the other things which they unfold in an elaborate and forced manner, so as to affirm that there was some time in which Paul would not dare to say: "I live, now not I, but Christ lives in me" (Gal. 2:20); and this: "Or do you seek a proof of him who speaks in me, Christ" (2 Cor. 13:3)? What sort of proof of Christ is it, they say, to hear: "The cloak which I left at Troas with Carpus, when you come bring with you" (2 Tim. 4:13)? And this to the Galatians: "Would that they were even cut off who trouble you" (Gal. 5:12). And in this very Epistle: "But at the same time also prepare me a lodging". And this, they say, happened in like manner not only to the apostles but also to the prophets. Hence it is quite often found written: "The word of the Lord came to Ezekiel" (Ezek. 22), or to any other of the prophets, because after the prophecy had been completed, returning again into himself, he became an ordinary man instead of a prophet; and in no one except our Lord Jesus Christ did the Holy Spirit abide permanently. This sign John the Baptist too had received: that he upon whom he saw the Holy Spirit descending and remaining in him, he should know to be the one (John 1). From this he shows that the Holy Spirit indeed descends upon many, but that this is the distinctive mark of the Saviour, that he abides permanently in him. By these and other arguments of this kind they hold either that the Epistle which is written to Philemon is not Paul's, or that, even if it is Paul's, it has nothing that can edify us; and that it was rejected by most of the ancients, since it was written merely for the purpose of commending, not of teaching. But on the contrary, those who defend it as of genuine authority say that it would never have been received throughout the whole world by all the churches unless it were believed to be Paul the apostle's. And by this rule, they say, those men ought not to receive even the second Epistle to Timothy, and that to the Galatians, from which he himself also published examples of human weakness: "The cloak which I left at Troas with Carpus, when you come bring with you"; and: "Would that they were cut off who trouble you". Very many things are found both in Romans and in the letters to the other churches, and especially to the Corinthians, dictated in a more relaxed way and in almost everyday speech, in which the Apostle says: "But to the rest I say, not the Lord". These too, because they contain something of the sort, must either not be thought epistles of Paul; or, if these are received, that to Philemon must also be received, on the precedent of similar letters already received. And those men, they say, err greatly and naively if they think that buying food, preparing a lodging, procuring clothes, is a sin, and assert that the Holy Spirit is put to flight if for a little while we serve the necessities of the poor body. "Do not", says the Apostle, "grieve the Holy Spirit, in whom you were sealed in the day of redemption" (Eph. 4:30). By what works the Holy Spirit is grieved the prophet records, having set out many vices and sins in order, and adding at the end: "In all these you grieved me". Otherwise, would offering a cup of cold water, washing feet, sacrificing a calf, preparing a meal, be a sin, when we know that through these things certain people are adopted as sons of God? This is not the time to answer everything, since we have not brought forward everything that they are accustomed to propose. But if they do not think that small things belong to those who own the great things as well, then, according to Valentinus, Marcion and Apelles, they must bring in for me one Creator of the ant, of worms, gnats and locusts, and another of heaven, earth, sea and the angels. Or rather, is it not a mark of the same power not to withhold in lesser things also the skill which you have exercised in greater? And since we have made mention of Marcion, let them be taught that the Epistle to Philemon is Paul's at least on Marcion's authority. Although he either did not receive the other Epistles of the same Apostle, or changed and gnawed away certain things in them, on this one alone he did not dare to lay hands, because its brevity defended it. But they seem to me, while they accuse the epistle of simplicity, to betray their own lack of skill, not understanding what power and wisdom lies hidden in its individual words. These things, while you pray, and with the Holy Spirit himself, by whom they were written, prompting us, we shall try to explain in their places. But if brevity is held in contempt, let Obadiah, Nahum, Zephaniah and the others of the twelve prophets be despised, in whom the things that are related are so wonderful and so great that you would not know whether you ought to admire in them the brevity of the words or the greatness of the meanings. But if those who reject the Epistle to Philemon understood this, they would never despise brevity, which, in place of the long-trailing burdens of the Law, has been written with the beauty of the Gospel, since the Lord makes a word shortened and completed upon the earth. But now the very words of the Apostle are to be set down, which begin thus.
Commentary on Philemon

Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy the brother, to Philemon the beloved and our fellow worker, and to Apphia the sister, and to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the church that is in your house: grace to you and peace from God our Father and our Lord Jesus Christ.

You have been pleased to have me dictate to you on the Epistles of Paul in a back-to-front and inverted order. For when you, O Paula and Eustochium, often asked me to do it, and I stubbornly refused, you compelled me at least to discuss a short one, and one which seemed to you the last in sense and order as well as in the number of its verses. I shall therefore attempt at the end what belongs to the beginning. Another commentator would ask at once, in his introduction to the Apostle, why, or at what time, or by whose naming, he received the name of Paul in place of Saul. I am now compelled to do this, although before this day I had never dared to utter even a mu about him, as the saying goes. Nor indeed should it be thought, as the simpler Latins read it, that he was formerly called Saulus and not Saul; for he was of the tribe of Benjamin, in which this name was quite familiar. Indeed, that well-known Saul, king of Judea, the persecutor of David, was also of the tribe of Benjamin. But as for his being called Saulus by us, it is no wonder that Hebrew names are declined after the likeness of the Greek and Roman cases, so that just as Josephus is said for Joseph, and Jacobus for Jacob, so Saulus too is said for Saul in our language and speech. The question, then, is why, or at whose command, he either lost his old name or took a new one. That Abram should be called Abraham was accomplished by God's bidding (Gen. 17, etc.); that the name Sarai should become Sarah was likewise God's command. And to come to the New Testament: that Simon should receive the name of Peter (Mark 3), and that the sons of Zebedee should be called BANE REEM (בני רעם), that is, "sons of thunder", was ordained by the voice of our Lord Jesus Christ (ibid.). But why he was called Paul instead of Saul, no Scripture records. I shall therefore act boldly, but perhaps truly, in setting out my conjectures from the Acts of the Apostles. We read in them that the Holy Spirit said at Antioch: "Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have taken them up. Then, fasting and praying and laying hands on them, they sent them away" (Acts 13:3 ff.). They went down to Seleucia of Syria and sailed to Salamis of Cyprus, which is now called Constantia. They had John with them in the ministry (on whose account a quarrel edifying to the Church was later stirred up). When they had travelled through the whole island and come as far as Paphos, they found a certain magician, a false prophet named Bar-Jesus, with the proconsul Sergius Paulus, a prudent man. The proconsul summoned Barnabas and Saul and desired to hear the word of God from them. So when the magician resisted and was perverting Sergius from the right faith, "Saul" (says Scripture) "who is also Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looking upon him said: O full of all guile and all deceit, son of the devil, enemy of all justice, do you not cease to subvert the right ways of the Lord? And now behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you shall be blind, not seeing the sun for a time. And immediately a mist and darkness fell upon him, and going about he sought someone to give him his hand. Then the proconsul, when he had seen what was done, believed, marvelling at the teaching of the Lord. And when Paul and those who were with him had sailed from Paphos, they came to Perga of Pamphylia". Note carefully that it is here that he first received the name of Paul. Scipio, having subdued Africa, took for himself the name of Africanus; Metellus, having subjugated the island of Crete, brought back to his family the distinction of Creticus; and Roman emperors down to the present day are styled Adiabenicus, Parthicus and Sarmaticus from the nations they have subdued. In the same way Saul, sent to preach to the Gentiles, brought back the trophies of his victory from the first spoil of the Church, the proconsul Sergius Paulus, and raised his standard, so that he was called Paul instead of Saul. But if the meaning of the name is also sought, Paul in Hebrew means "wonderful". And truly it is a wonder that after being Saul, which means "sought after" (because he had been demanded by the devil to harass the Church), he should become, from a persecutor, a vessel of election. This has been discussed at greater length perhaps than was fitting, but necessarily. As for what follows, prisoner of Jesus Christ: in no Epistle has he used this title, although in the body of the Epistles, namely those to the Ephesians, the Philippians and the Colossians, he testifies that he is in chains for his confession. And it seems to me a mark of greater loftiness to call himself a prisoner of Jesus Christ than an apostle. For the apostles gloried that they had been worthy to suffer insult for the name of Jesus Christ (Acts 5:41); but the authority of the chains was necessary. Since he was about to plead for Onesimus, he had to plead as one who could obtain what he asked. Happy indeed is he who glories not in wisdom, not in riches, not in eloquence and worldly power, but in the sufferings of Christ. With such words he also concludes his Epistle to the Galatians: "For the rest," he says, "let no one trouble me; for I bear the marks of our Lord Jesus Christ in my body" (Gal. 6). Not everyone who is a prisoner, however, is a prisoner of Christ. Whoever is bound for the name of Christ and for confessing him, he is truly called a prisoner of Jesus Christ; and only that shed blood makes a martyr which is poured out for the name of Christ. He writes to Philemon, then, as a prisoner in prison at Rome, at the time when, it seems to me, the Epistles to the Philippians, Colossians and Ephesians were dictated. I place the Epistle to the Philippians there for this reason: first, because he writes with Timothy alone, as he also does in this Epistle. Next, because he says that his chains have become manifest for Christ throughout the whole praetorium. What the praetorium is, he indicates at the end of that same Epistle: "All the saints greet you, but especially those who are of Caesar's household". Sent to prison by Caesar and having become better known to his household, he made the persecutor's house a church of Christ. Then he says: "But some proclaim Christ out of contention, not sincerely, thinking to stir up affliction for my chains" (Phil. 1:17). Further, the opening to the Colossians is also similar: "Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, and Timothy the brother". And in what follows: "Of which I, Paul, have been made a minister, who now rejoice in sufferings for you, and fill up in my flesh what is lacking of the sufferings of Christ, for his body, which is the Church" (Col. 1:2, 23, 24). And at the end: "My greeting by the hand of Paul. Be mindful of my chains" (Col. 4:18). I cite this so that we may know that these Epistles too were dictated from prison and in chains. But the Epistle to the Colossians has this peculiar feature, that the same Onesimus who is now commended to Philemon was also the bearer of that letter. Accordingly he says: "All that concerns me Tychicus will make known to you, the dearest brother and faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord, whom I have sent to you for this purpose, that he may know what concerns you and comfort your hearts, with Onesimus, the dearest and faithful brother, who is one of you" (ibid. 7, 8). Now Philemon, to whom this epistle is written, is the master of Onesimus, or rather has begun to be his brother in the Lord. And the Colossians are told that Onesimus is one of them. If so, reason itself and the order of things lead us to conclude two things: that Philemon too was a Colossian, and that Onesimus carried the letter common to the whole church at the same time as he took up the private letter commending him to his master. There is also another indication: in this same epistle Archippus too is named, to whom the present letter is written along with Philemon. "Say", he says, "to Archippus: See to the ministry which you have received from the Lord, that you fulfil it". What is the ministry which Archippus received from the Lord? In the letter to Philemon we read: "And to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the church that is in your house". From this I think that he was bishop of the Colossian church and is admonished to preside over it zealously and diligently, as a preacher of the Gospel. Or, if that is not so, this suffices me for the present: that Philemon and Archippus, and Onesimus himself who carried the letters, were Colossians, and that the four Epistles (as we said before) were written at the same time. I place the Epistle to the Ephesians there for this reason. Here too he says that he is a prisoner for Christ. At the end of this Epistle he also enjoins the same things he had commanded the Colossians: that wives be subject to their husbands, and husbands love their wives; that children obey their parents; that fathers not provoke their children to anger; that slaves obey their masters according to the flesh; that masters lay aside threats and grant their slaves what is just. And at the very end he concludes his Epistle thus: "What I am doing Tychicus will make known to you, the dearest brother and faithful minister in the Lord, whom I have sent to you for this very purpose, that you may know what concerns me, and that he may comfort your hearts". Now Tychicus is the one who is also sent to the Colossians with Onesimus, and he had Onesimus as his travelling companion at the time when Onesimus was carrying the letter to Philemon.

And Timothy the brother. In other epistles Sosthenes and Silvanus are associated with him, and sometimes Timothy the brother. In only four is Timothy named alone, because they were dictated either at the same time, or with Timothy and the others present. I think this was done for a twofold reason. First, so that the Epistle might have greater authority, since it was not written by one man. Second, there was no rivalry among the apostles: if perhaps, while Paul was dictating, the Spirit had suggested something to another, Paul added it without any vexation to the letter he was dictating. He did so in accordance with what he himself enjoined on the Corinthians: if, while one is prophesying, something is revealed to another, he who was prophesying first should be silent (1 Cor. 14). Thus he too fulfilled his own precept in deed, and because of the few things he had added at another's suggestion, he headed the epistle as another's as well as his own. To Philemon, he says, the beloved. The Greek does not have ἠγαπημένῳ, which is rendered "beloved" (dilectus), but ἀγαπητῷ, that is, "lovable" (diligibilis). Between beloved (dilectus) and lovable (diligibilis) there is this difference: even one who does not deserve love can be called beloved, but only one who is loved for his merit is lovable. Thus we are commanded to love even our enemies, who are beloved, but not lovable. For we love them, not because they deserve to be loved, but because we are commanded not to hold them in hatred. Again, what is set down in the title of the forty-fourth Psalm, "for the beloved", is better in the Greek, "for the lovable"; and this passage is most plainly understood of Christ. The Jews think that Solomon is called IDIDIA (ידידיה), that is, "loved by God", because that name was given him by God on account of his wisdom (2 Sam. 12). Yet who can more truly be called loved by God than he of whom the Father speaks in the Gospel: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him" (Luke 9:36)? So also in Isaiah it is written thus: "I will sing to the beloved a song of the lovable one for my vineyard. A vineyard was made for the beloved" (Isa. 5:1). The circumcision thought that this was to be understood of the Jewish people, and so struck against the stone of stumbling and the rock of scandal. They did not reflect that the vineyard transplanted from Egypt is the house of Israel, and that it is Christ who is here called either lovable or beloved. For he both deserves to be loved by the saints, and the saints love him, offering him love rather than demanding any rewards for their love. Paul and Timothy therefore write to Philemon, dearest and fellow worker; he is called dearest for this reason, that he is engaged in the same work of Christ.
Commentary on Philemon

According to the Jews, Paul means "admirable"; Timothy, "beneficent"; Philemon, "wonderfully gifted" or "mouth of bread", from os "mouth", not os "bone"; Apphia, "continent" or "liberty"; Archippus, "length of work"; Onesimus, "answering"; Epaphras, "fruitful" and "seeing", or "growing up"; Mark, "exalted by commandment"; Aristarchus, "mountain of greater work"; Demas, "silent"; Luke, "himself rising up". If you wish to understand these names according to their meaning, it is not difficult to see that the admirable and beneficent one writes above all to him to whom all faults have been forgiven and whose mouth lies open to the heavenly bread. Next he writes to the continent woman, the free woman, and to the length of work, because he never desists from holy labour. He writes on behalf of him who answers to his own testimony. He writes also that greeting is given to him to whom the Epistle is specially dedicated, by growing fruitfulness. And the one who has been made more exalted through the commandments sends greeting, and the greeting comes from him who through greater works has grown up even into a mountain. It comes also from him who set a guard on his mouth and a fortified door on his lips, who perhaps kept silent for this reason, that he had for a little while abandoned the Apostle. And last, it comes from him who, rising up through himself, is daily increased and makes progress, while the world is filled with his Gospel, and he grows as often as, being heard and read, he edifies.
Commentary on Philemon

However, although Philemon was not a cleric, he nevertheless participated in the needs of the Church out of devotion, hence he says that he is a participant in these labors. For there are indeed many who, although worthy, excuse themselves, judging themselves unworthy of such a ministry; hence they appear truly worthy.
Homily on Philemon 1

"And to our beloved Apphia."

It seems to me that she was his partner in life. Observe the humility of Paul; he both joins Timothy with him in his request, and asks not only the husband, but the wife also, and some one else, perhaps a friend.
Homily on Philemon 1

"And Archippus," he says, "our fellow-soldier."

Not wishing to effect such things by command, and not taking it ill, if he did not immediately comply with his request; but he begs them to do what a stranger might have done to aid his request. For not only the being requested by many, but the petition being urged to many, contributes to its being granted. And on this account he says, "And Archippus our fellow-soldier." If thou art a fellow-soldier, thou oughtest also to take a concern in these things. But this is the Archippus, about whom he says in his Epistle to the Colossians, "Say to Archippus, Take heed to the ministry which thou hast received in the Lord, that thou fulfill it." (Col. iv. 17.) It seems to me too, that he, whom he joins with him in this request, was also one of the Clergy. And he calls him his fellow-soldier, that he may by all means cooperate with him.
Homily on Philemon 1

"And to the Church in thy house."

Here he has not omitted even the slaves. For he knew that often even the words of slaves have power to overthrow their master; and more especially when his request was in behalf of a slave. And perhaps it was they particularly who exasperated him. He does not suffer them therefore to fall into envy, having honored them by including them in a salutation with their masters. And neither does he allow the master to take offense. For if he had made mention of them by name, perhaps he would have been angry. And if he had not mentioned them at all, he might have been displeased. Observe therefore how prudently he has found a way by his manner of mentioning them, both to honor them by his mention of them, and not to wound him. For the name of the "Church" does not suffer masters to be angry, even though they are reckoned together with their servants. For the Church knows not the distinction of master and servant. By good actions and by sins she defines the one and the other. If then it is a Church, be not displeased that thy slave is saluted with thee. "For in Christ Jesus there is neither bond nor free." (Gal. iii. 28.)
Commentary on Philemon

They write also to Apphia the sister, who had in her nothing of a false and feigned sisterhood. And they write to Archippus the fellow soldier: I think that, fighting with Paul and Timothy against adversaries for the name of Christ, he proved victorious, and is therefore now called fellow soldier because he prevailed in the same contest and war. It is written also to the church that is in his house. But this is ambiguous: is it the church in the house of Archippus, or the one in the house of Philemon? It seems to me that it should be referred not to the person of Archippus but to that of Philemon, to whom the epistle itself is assigned. For although Paul and Timothy write jointly to Philemon, Apphia, Archippus and the church, yet what follows proves that Paul alone is writing to Philemon, one conversing with one: "I give thanks to my God always, and making remembrance of you". You will be able to find this manner of writing in a number of his epistles: several persons, writing to several, are set down in the preface, but afterwards, throughout the whole body of the Epistle, one alone is brought in as discoursing. Writing to the Galatians, the Apostle says that in the faith of Christ it makes no difference whether one is a Gentile or a Jew, man or woman, slave or free (Gal. 3:28); this too becomes clear in this place. For between two men, and apostolic men, between Paul's fellow worker and his fellow soldier, the name of Apphia is inserted in the middle, so that, supported on either side by such company, she may be seen to hold her rank by merit, not by sex.
Commentary on Galatians

The benefit of both the Father and the Son reveals the upliftment of the human race. It does not indicate a lesser Son when it calls him our Lord, nor a greater Father when it calls him our God. Because the Father will not be a true God unless he is also Lord, and the Son will not be a true Lord unless he is also God.
Homily on Philemon 1

"Grace to you, and peace."

By mentioning "grace," he brings his own sins to his remembrance. Consider, he says, how great things God has pardoned in thee, how by grace thou art saved. Imitate thy Lord. And he prays for "peace" to him; and naturally: for it comes then when we imitate Him, then grace abides. Since even that servant who was unmerciful to his fellow-servants, until he demanded the hundred pence, had the grace of his master abiding on him. But when he made that demand, it was taken from him, and he was delivered to the tormentors.
Commentary on Philemon

As for his saying, Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, it is still written by two to several. In almost all the Epistles the opening is the same, calling down upon them grace and peace from God the Father and Christ the Lord. From this it is shown that the nature of the Son and of the Father is one, since the Son can bestow what the Father bestows, and the Father is said to bestow what the Son bestows. Now grace is that by which we are saved through no merit or work. Peace is that by which we have been reconciled to God through Christ, as in the passage: "We beseech you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God" (2 Cor. 5:20).
Homily on Philemon 2

He does not immediately at the commencement ask the favor, but having first admired the man, and having praised him for his good actions, and having shown no small proof of his love, that he always made mention of him in his prayers, and having said that many are refreshed by him, and that he is obedient and complying in all things; then he puts it last of all, by this particularly putting him to the blush. For if others obtain the things which they ask, much more Paul. If coming before others, he was worthy to obtain, much more when he comes after others, and asks a thing not pertaining to himself, but in behalf of another. Then, that he may not seem to have written on this account only, and that no one may say, "If it were not for Onesimus thou wouldest not have written," see how he assigns other causes also of his Epistle. In the first place manifesting his love, then also desiring that a lodging may be prepared for him.
Commentary on Philemon

I give thanks to my God always, making remembrance of you in my prayers, hearing of your love and the faith which you have in the Lord Jesus and in all his saints: that the sharing of your faith may become evident in the full knowledge of every good which is in you in Christ.

These words he now speaks not as Paul and Timothy to Philemon and the rest, but as Paul alone to Philemon alone: I give thanks, he says, to my God always making remembrance of you in my prayers. It is said ambiguously, however, whether he gives thanks to his God always, or makes remembrance of him in his prayers always. And both can be understood. For he who instructs others to give thanks to God in all things can be hemmed in by no straits so tight that he does not himself render thanks to God always. But if Paul always prayed for the saints and for all the better sort (and Philemon too is holy, having in himself such faith and love that he was known to him not only by report but also by deed), it is credible that Paul also prayed always for Philemon. He prayed, namely, that the faith and love which Philemon had in Christ and in all his saints might be preserved by Christ's mercy, through the sharing of faith and the operation of full knowledge in every good.
Homily on Philemon 2

"Hearing," he says, "of thy love."

This is wonderful, and much greater than if being present he had seen it when he was present. For it is plain that from its being excessive it had become manifest, and had reached even to Paul. And yet the distance between Rome and Phrygia was not small. For he seems to have been there from the mention of Archippus. For the Colossians were of Phrygia, writing to whom he said, "When this Epistle is read among you, cause that it be read also in the Church of the Laodiceans, and that ye likewise read the Epistle from Laodicea." (Col. iv. 16.) And this is a city of Phrygia.
Commentary on Philemon

And concerning the love which he had in Christ Jesus and in all his saints, the interpretation is indeed not difficult: it is the love by which, after God, we bid [men] to love our neighbors too. Now the question is this: how can anyone have the same faith in Christ Jesus and in his saints? For, by ἀπὸ κοινοῦ, the phrase sounds both ways: the love which you have in the Lord Jesus and in all his saints, and the faith which you have in the Lord Jesus and in all his saints. To expound this passage let us take an example from Exodus: "The people believed God and Moses his servant" (Exod. 19). One and the same belief is directed to Moses and to God, so that the people who believed in the Lord is said to have believed equally in the servant. And this holds not only in Moses but in all his saints, so that whoever has believed God cannot receive faith in him in any other way unless he also believes in his saints. For that love and faith toward God is not perfect which is thinned by hatred and unbelief toward his ministers. What I mean is this. Someone has believed in God the Creator. He cannot believe unless he has first believed that what is written about his saints is true: that Adam was formed by God; that Eve was fashioned from his rib and side; that Enoch was translated; that Noah alone was saved when the world was shipwrecked; that Abraham, the first to be commanded to go out from his land and his kindred, left to his descendants the circumcision which he had received as a sign of the offspring to come; that Isaac was offered as a victim, and that a ram, sacrificed in his place and crowned with thorns, foreshadowed the Lord's passion; that Moses and Aaron afflicted Egypt with ten plagues; that at the voice and prayers of Joshua the son of Nun the sun stood still in Gibeon, and the moon in the valley of Aijalon. It would be long to run through all the deeds of the Judges, and to draw the whole story of Samson to the mystery of the true sun (for that is what his name signifies). I shall come to the books of Kings: when at harvest time, at Samuel's entreaty, rains and streams suddenly poured down from heaven; and David was anointed king; and Nathan and Gad prophesied mysteries; when Elijah was caught up in a fiery chariot, and Elisha, with a double spirit, though dead raised the dead. Unless one has believed all these things and the rest that are written about the saints, he will not be able to believe in the God of the saints. Nor can he be brought to faith in the Old Testament unless he has accepted as true whatever the history narrates about the patriarchs and prophets and other distinguished men: so that from the faith of the Law he may come to the faith of the Gospel, and the righteousness of God may be revealed in him from faith to faith, as it is written: "But the just lives by faith" (Hab. 2). It is also commanded in another place: "Be holy, because I am holy, says the Lord your God" (Lev. 19:2). The same holiness is owed to the servants and to the Lord: for both he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one. Let us not think it slight praise of Philemon that he has the same faith in the saints as in God. He who believes God to be holy certainly does not err. But if anyone believes a man who is not holy to be holy, and joins him to fellowship with God, he violates Christ, of whose body we are all members. "He who says", he says, "that the just is unjust and the unjust just, both are abominable before God" (Prov. 7:15). Likewise he who says that the holy is not holy, and again asserts that the unholy is holy, is abominable before God. All believers, according to the Apostle, are made the body of Christ (1 Cor. 6). Whoever errs and slips with regard to the body of Christ, asserting that a member of it is holy when it is not, or not holy when it is holy, see what a charge he becomes liable to: "Woe", says Isaiah, "to those who call sweet bitter and bitter sweet, making darkness light and light darkness" (Isa. 5:20). Sweet, I think, is holiness; bitter is what is contrary to holiness. Likewise holiness can be understood as light, and darkness as what is contrary to holiness. Which of us, do you think, though a moneychanger skilled in testing coins, will not err in discerning the saints?
Homily on Philemon 2

I pray, he says, "that the communication of thy faith may become effectual in the knowledge of every good thing which is in Christ Jesus." Dost thou see him first giving, before he receives, and before he asks a favor himself bestowing a much greater one of his own? "That the communication of thy faith," he says, "may become effectual by the acknowledging of every good thing which is in you in Christ Jesus"; that is, that thou mayest attain all virtue, that nothing may be deficient. For so faith becomes effectual, when it is accompanied with works. For "without works faith is dead." (Jas. ii. 26.) And he has not said, "Thy faith," but "the communication of thy faith," connecting it with himself, and showing that it is one body, and by this particularly making him ashamed to refuse. If thou art a partaker, he says, with respect to the faith, thou oughtest to communicate also with respect to other things.
Commentary on Philemon

He who has equal love and faith in God and in his saints ought to have a sharing of that faith which is not unequal: so that as he believes and loves, so he may complete his love and faith in deed. Hence he says: May become evident in the full knowledge of every good; or, as it stands better in the Greek, "effective". For ἐνεργής can properly be rendered effective or operative: so that we may not merely believe that faith and love in God and in his saints can suffice for us, but that what we believe may be fulfilled in deed. It can happen, however, that someone has faith and completes it in deed, but simply and barely, without having full knowledge or knowledge of it, according to that saying of the Apostle: "I confess that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge" (Rom. 10:2). There are today many among the simple who do works of righteousness and have no knowledge of the things they themselves do. Hence he added: That the sharing of your faith may become operative in the full knowledge of every good. By what great steps and what great leaps does the apostolic word stretch itself toward higher things? Someone has love and faith in God and in his saints, but perhaps he does not share it with all in an equal balance. Perhaps he shares it with all, but does not carry it out in deed. Someone may fulfil it in will and in deed, yet he cannot have a perfect understanding of his own actions. Let there also be such a one as has both the work and the knowledge, yet he does not have the full knowledge of every good. For though he performs many things justly, gently and zealously, he is unequal in some part to his own virtues. Is not Philemon such a one? For he has the sharing of an operative faith and love in the full knowledge of every good. And since this is in the apostles, let us not think it perfect merely because it is in them, but entire in this, that it is Christ's. So whatever good is both praised in Philemon and taken from the example of the apostles is good for this reason, that it is drawn from the fountain of Christ.
Commentary on Philemon

It is evident that he expresses himself as being joyful because he was ministering to the needs of the saints: from which he rejoices even more, being certain that he was obeying his commands, whom he knows to be superior.
Homily on Philemon 2

Nothing so shames us into giving, as to bring forward the kindnesses bestowed on others, and particularly when a man is more entitled to respect than they. And he has not said, "If you do it to others, much more to me"; but he has insinuated the same thing, though he has contrived to do it in another and a more gracious manner.

"I had joy," that is, thou hast given me confidence from the things which thou hast done to others. "And consolation," that is, we are not only gratified, but we are also comforted. For they are members of us. If then there ought to be such an agreement, that in the refreshing of any others who are in affliction, though we obtain nothing, we should be delighted on their account, as if it were one body that was benefited; much more if you shall refresh us also. And he has not said, "Because thou yieldest, and compliest," but even more vehemently and emphatically, "because the bowels of the Saints," as if it were for a darling child fondly loved by its parents, so that this love and affection shows that he also is exceedingly beloved by them.
Commentary on Philemon

For we have had great joy and consolation in your love, because the bowels of the saints have found rest through you, brother.

He drives home and explains more fully why he had said: "I give thanks to my God, always making remembrance of you in my prayers". For it was indeed fitting to give thanks to God for the love of Philemon, who, by receiving them, had refreshed the inner affection of the heart and the deep recesses of the saints' souls. And this is an apostolic idiom: he always says "bowels" when he wishes to show the full love of the mind. Therefore, rejoicing with those who rejoice, and believing that he himself had been refreshed along with those who had found rest, he has a joy that is not passing and light, nor such as might come about by chance. It is great, and as surpassing as the love that was in Philemon. That joy was increased by the consolation over Philemon's love, a consolation coming down, full, from the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation.
Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians

I do not issue orders to you, as if I were some great person. For though I am bound for the name [of Christ], I am not yet perfect in Jesus Christ. For now I begin to be a disciple, and I speak to you as fellow-disciples with me. For it was needful for me to have been stirred up by you in faith, exhortation, patience, and long-suffering. But inasmuch as love suffers me not to be silent in regard to you, I have therefore taken upon me first to exhort you that ye would all run together in accordance with the will of God. For even Jesus Christ, our inseparable life, is the [manifested] will of the Father; as also bishops, settled everywhere to the utmost bounds [of the earth], are so by the will of Jesus Christ.
Commentary on Philemon

As much as reason required, it was fitting to command a disciple as a master by the authority of the apostolic faith: but because Philemon was a good man, he entices him through affection to obedience, as if he were a companion in age, and a prisoner of Jesus Christ, that is, bound by the affairs of the Lord, or subject to his name in chains, just as the apostles themselves were. For indeed, there were Judas and Silas, who were leaders among the brothers, being from the common people, they had committed themselves to the Lord's work (Acts 15:22 and following); so that they could work together with the apostles for the sake of faith in God. Hence, Silas is found to be a partner in the apostle's labors.
Homily on Philemon 2

Observe how cautious he is, lest any of the things which were spoken even from exceeding love should so strike the hearer, as that he should be hurt. For this reason before he says, "to enjoin thee," since it was offensive, although, as spoken out of love, it was more proper to soothe him, yet nevertheless from an excess of delicacy, he as it were corrects it by saying, "Having confidence," by which he implies that Philemon was a great man, that is "Thou hast given confidence to us." And not only that, but adding the expression "in Christ," by which he shows that it was not that he was more illustrious in the world, not that he was more powerful, but it was on account of his faith in Christ,-then he also adds, "to enjoin thee," and not that only, but "that which is convenient," that is, a reasonable action. And see out of how many things he brings proof for this. Thou doest good to others, he says, and to me, and for Christ's sake, and that the thing is reasonable, and that love giveth...
Commentary on Philemon

Wherefore, having much confidence in Christ Jesus to command you what is profitable for love's sake, I rather beseech, since you are such a one, as Paul an old man, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ.

Many praises of Philemon have been set out beforehand. The matter for which he is asked is also such as to be useful both to the one who grants it and to the one who asks. Paul therefore could have commanded rather than requested. This came from that confidence: one who had accomplished such great works for Christ's sake could surely not be unequal to himself in other matters. But he prefers to ask rather than to order, having first set forth the great authority of the one who asks, by which it is at once the Apostle who beseeches, and an old man, and a prisoner of Jesus Christ. Now the whole matter for which he asks is this. Onesimus, Philemon's slave, heaping theft upon flight, had pilfered certain things belonging to the household. Setting out from there for Italy, so that he could not be caught so easily close at hand, he had squandered his master's money in riotous living. Lest anyone think this rashly said and invented by us at our pleasure, let him learn it from what follows. For Paul would never say: "If he has done you any harm or owes you anything, charge this to me: I Paul have written it with my own hand, I will repay." Nor would he become guarantor for property taken away unless what had been taken had been squandered. This man, then, when Paul was in prison at Rome for confessing Christ, believed in Christ. Baptized by him, he wiped away the stains of his former life by a worthy penitence, so much so that the witness of his conversion was that apostle who had once rebuked Peter for not walking with a straight foot in the truth of the Gospel (Gal. 2). So far, therefore, as concerns the sin and the crime by which he had wronged his master, he does not deserve pardon. But so far as concerns the testimony of the Apostle, who knows him to be fully converted, great weight presses upon the one who is asked, that the man who from a runaway slave and robber had been made a minister of the Apostle (and what other ministry does the Apostle have but that of the Gospel of Christ Jesus?) should now be pardoned, no longer as by a master but as by a fellow servant and fellow evangelist, since he was likewise a servant and minister of Christ.
