He is called younger still, who had not yet reached the mature age of the white-haired faith, who had not yet grown into a perfect man, into that full measure of the age of the fullness of Christ (Eph. IV, 13). Finally, he is only called young there (Acts VII, 57), where he was keeping the garments of those stoning Stephen. And for this reason, he desired Philemon to be like him not in his youth but in his old age, as he wrote: I beg you even more, now that I am old like Paul (Philem. 9). Therefore, he advises that younger widows should be avoided (I Tim. V, 11), not because of their age but because of a certain lasciviousness of youthful transgressions and immaturity of virtue. However, there is greater praise for chastity in a young person than in an old person.
Homily on Philemon 2

As if he had said, I know indeed that I can effect it by commanding with much authority, from things which have already taken place. But because I am very solicitous about this matter, "I beseech thee." He shows both these things at once; that he has confidence in him, for he commands him; and that he is exceedingly concerned about the matter, wherefore he beseeches him.

"Being such an one," he says, "as Paul the aged." Strange! how many things are here to shame him into compliance! Paul, from the quality of his person, from his age, because he was old, and from what was more just than all, because he was also "a prisoner of Jesus Christ."

For who would not receive with open arms a combatant who had been crowned? Who seeing him bound for Christ's sake, would not have granted him ten thousand favors? By so many considerations having previously soothed his mind, he has not immediately introduced the name, but defers making so great a request. For you know what are the minds of masters towards slaves that have run away; and particularly when they have done this with robbery, even if they have good masters, how their anger is increased. This anger then having taken all these pains to soothe, and having first persuaded him readily to serve him in anything whatever, and having prepared his soul to all obedience, then he introduces his request, and says, "I beseech thee," and with the addition of praises, "for my son whom I have begotten in my bonds."
The Seven Books on the Incarnation of the Lord, Book 4, Chapter 11

As there are chains of coercion, so too there are chains of love, as the Lord says: "I drew them with chains of love." For indeed great are these chains, and chains of ineffable love, for those who are bound with them rejoice in their fetters. Do you want to know whether this is true? Hear how the Apostle Paul exults and rejoices in his chains, when he says: "I therefore a prisoner in the Lord beseech you." And again: "I beseech thee, whereas thou art such an one as Paul the aged, and now a prisoner also of Jesus Christ." You see how he rejoiced in the dignity of his chains, by the example of which he actually stirred up others. But there can be no doubt that where there is single-minded love of the Lord, there is also single-minded delight in chains worn for the Lord's sake: as it is written: "But the multitude of the believers was of one heart and one soul."
Commentary on Philemon

It is not a great thing to humble oneself when one is lowly, but it is commendable for a noble man to humble himself. Therefore, the Apostle asks him, to whom he has the authority to command, to be in all things a model for the advancement of merits. Therefore, when Onesimus, a fugitive, returned to seek divine assistance, the Apostle baptized him while he was in custody in the city of Rome, seeing the hope of usefulness in him.
Homilies on Ephesians 8

And mark, on the other hand, the fervency of Paul also. Bound, scourged, thus he preached the Gospel. Oh, that blessed chain, with how great travail did it travail that night, what children did it bring forth! Yea of them too may he say, "Whom I have begotten in my bonds." Mark thou, how he glories, and will have the children thus begotten, to be on that account the more illustrious! Mark thou, how transcendant is the glory of those bonds, in that they give lustre not only to him that wore them, but also to them who were on that occasion begotten by him. They have some advantage, who were begotten in Paul's bonds, I say not in respect of grace, (for grace is one and the same,) nor in respect of remission, (for remission is one and the same to all,) but in that they are thus from the very outset taught to rejoice and to glory in such things.
Homily on Philemon 2

Again the chains are mentioned to shame him into compliance, and then the name. For he has not only extinguished his anger, but has caused him to be delighted. For I would not have called him my son, he says, if he were not especially profitable. What I called Timothy, that I call him also. And repeatedly showing his affection, he urges him by the very period of his new birth, "I have begotten him in my bonds," he says, so that on this account also he was worthy to obtain much honor, because he was begotten in his very conflicts, in his trials in the cause of Christ.
Commentary on Philemon

I beseech you for my son, whom I have begotten in chains, Onesimus, who was once unprofitable to you, but now is profitable both to you and to me: whom I have sent back to you. But do you receive him, that is, my bowels, whom I had wished to keep with me, so that in your stead he might minister to me in the chains of the Gospel.

Wishing to obtain what he asks, he declares that he is now pleading not for Philemon's slave but for his own son, and for that son whom he had begotten in the chains of the Gospel, that is, the chains he was enduring for the Gospel of Christ. Before, this man had been unprofitable only to his master (for a slave who is a thief and a runaway has harmed no one but his master). Now, on the contrary, he is useful to his master himself and to Paul, and through Paul to the rest. By this compensation of usefulness he deserves more love than he had before deserved hatred. Hence he says: Who was once unprofitable to you. To you, he says, alone, not to the rest; but now profitable both to me and to you. He is profitable to his master in this, that he could also serve Paul in his master's stead; and profitable to Paul in this, that while Paul was held in prison and in chains, he could minister to him in the Gospel. At the same time we must marvel at the greatness of soul of the Apostle, and at his mind burning toward Christ. He is held in prison, he is bound tight with chains, he is hemmed in by the squalor of his body, by separation from those dear to him, by the darkness of punishment; and yet he does not feel the injury, he is not tormented by pain, he knows nothing else but to think about the Gospel of Christ. He knew that a slave, he knew that a runaway, he knew that one who had once been a robber had been converted to the faith of Christ. It is a matter of great labor for such a man to persevere in what he has begun. Therefore he presses home and repeats "his son," and "the son of his chains," and "the minister of the Gospel to one placed in chains." He does this so that Philemon, whom he had prudently and by way of accommodation praised so highly in the preface, would not dare to refuse, lest he seem unworthy of his own praises.
Commentary on Philemon

Therefore, when Onesimus, a fugitive, returned to seek divine assistance, the Apostle baptized him while he was in custody in the city of Rome, seeing the hope of usefulness in him. He commends him in such a way that he indicates his suitability to serve in secular as well as divine duties, having been transformed from useless to useful.
Homily on Philemon 2

See how great is his prudence, how he confesses the man's faults, and thereby extinguishes his anger. I know, he says, that he was unprofitable.

"But now" he will be "profitable to thee and to me."

He has not said he will be useful to thee, lest he should contradict it, but he has introduced his own person, that his hopes may seem worthy of credit, "But now," he says, "profitable to thee and to me." For if he was profitable to Paul, who required so great strictness, much more would he be so to his master.
Homily on Philemon 2

By this also he has quenched his anger, by delivering him up. For masters are then most enraged, when they are entreated for the absent, so that by this very act he mollified him the more.

"Thou therefore receive him, that is mine own bowels."

And again he has not given the bare name, but uses with it a word that might move him, which is more affectionate than son. He has said, "son," he has said, "I have begotten" him, so that it was probable he would love him much, because he begot him in his trials. For it is manifest that we are most inflamed with affection for those children, who have been born to us in dangers which we have escaped, as when the Scripture saith, "Woe, Barochabel!" and again when Rachel names Benjamin, "the son of my sorrow." (Gen. xxxv. 18.)

"Thou therefore," he says, "receive him, that is mine own bowels." He shows the greatness of his affection. He has not said, Take him back, he has not said, Be not angry, but "receive him"; that is, he is worthy not only of pardon, but of honor. Why? Because he is become the son of Paul.
Commentary on Philemon

As for his saying: But do you receive him, that is, my bowels, this is what I said a little earlier: bowels signify the inner affection of the heart and a full and heartfelt will, when the one who is asked receives everything whatever that is in us. Otherwise, all children are the bowels of their parents.
Homily on Philemon 2

Dost thou see after how much previous preparation, he has at length brought him honorably before his master, and observe with how much wisdom he has done this. See for how much he makes him answerable, and how much he honors the other. Thou hast found, he says, a way by which thou mayest through him repay thy service to me. Here he shows that he has considered his advantage more than that of his slave, and that he respects him exceedingly.
Homily on Philemon 2

This particularly flatters the person asked, when the thing being profitable in itself, it is brought out with his concurrence. For two good effects are produced thence, the one person gains, and the other is rendered more secure. And he has not said, That it should not be of necessity, but "as it were of necessity." For I knew, he says, that not having learnt it, but coming to know it at once, thou wouldest not have been angry, but nevertheless out of an excess of consideration, that it should "not be as it were of necessity."
Commentary on Philemon

But without your counsel I wished to do nothing, so that your good might not be as it were of necessity, but voluntary.

The question asked by very many, and very often taken up again, is why God, in making man, did not create him good and upright. It can be resolved from the present passage. For if God is good voluntarily, and not of necessity, then in making man he ought to have made him after his own image and likeness, that is, so that man too would be good voluntarily, and not of necessity. But those who assert that he ought to have been made such that he could not admit evil are saying this: he ought to have been made such that he would be good by necessity, and not by will. Yet if he had been made such as to accomplish good not by will but by necessity, he would not be like God, who is good because he wills it, not because he is compelled. From this it is manifest that they are demanding two things contrary to each other. For when they say, 'Man ought to have been made like God,' they are asking that he be made with free will, as God himself is. But when they infer, 'He ought to have been made such that he could not admit evil,' they impose upon him a necessity of good, and so they want man not to be made like God. So the Apostle Paul too could have kept Onesimus with him for his ministry without Philemon's will. But if he had done this without Philemon's will, it would indeed have been good, but not voluntary. And what was not voluntary would be shown on another ground not to be good. For nothing can be called good except what is spontaneous. From this we should consider the prudence of the Apostle: he sends the runaway slave back to his master for this reason, that he may be of profit to his master. He could not be of profit if he were kept while his master was absent. The question above, then, is resolved thus: God could have made man good without man's will. But if he had done this, the good would not have been voluntary, but of necessity. And what is good by necessity is not good, and on another ground is shown to be evil. Therefore, by leaving us to our own free choice, he made us all the more after his own image and likeness. And to be like God is absolutely good.
Homily on Philemon 2

He has well said, "perhaps," that the master may yield. For since the flight arose from perverseness, and a corrupt mind, and not from such intention, he has said, "perhaps." And he has not said, therefore he fled, but, therefore he was "separated," by a more fair sounding expression softening him the more. And he has not said, He separated himself, but, "he was separated." For it was not his own arrangement that he should depart either for this purpose or for that. Which also Joseph says, in making excuse for his brethren, "For God did send me hither" (Gen. xlv. 5), that is, He made use of their wickedness for a good end. "Therefore," he says, "he was parted for a season." Thus he contracts the time, acknowledges the offense, and turns it all to a providence. "That thou shouldest receive him," he says, "for ever," not for the present season only, but even for the future, that thou mightest always have him, no longer a slave, but more honorable than a slave. For thou wilt have a slave abiding with thee, more well-disposed than a brother, so that thou hast gained both in time, and in the quality of thy slave. For hereafter he will not run away. "That thou shouldest receive him," he says, "for ever," that is, have him again.

"No longer as a bond-servant, but more than a bond-servant, a brother beloved, especially to me."

Thou hast lost a slave for a short time, but thou wilt find a brother for ever, not only thy brother, but mine also. Here also there is much virtue. But if he is my brother, thou also wilt not be ashamed of him. By calling him his son, he hath shown his natural affection; and by calling him his brother, his great good will for him, and his equality in honor.
Commentary on Philemon

That you might receive him eternal. No one is the eternal master of his slave: for his power, and the condition of each of them, is ended by death. But Onesimus, who was made eternal through the faith of Christ, having received the spirit of liberty, began, from a slave, to be no longer a slave but a brother to Philemon, who is eternal because he too had believed in Christ: a dearest brother, an eternal brother; also to the eternal Apostle himself and to his master, to whom, as the condition of the flesh joined Onesimus before, so afterward the spirit joins him. And indeed then, when he was subject to him in the flesh, he was not joined to him in the Lord; but now he is joined to him both in the flesh and in the Lord. From this we understand that a slave who has believed in Christ is bound to his master by a twofold law: he is joined to him for a time by the necessity of the flesh, and united to him forever by the spirit.
Commentary on Philemon

For perhaps he therefore departed from you for an hour, that you might receive him eternal. No longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a dearest brother, especially to me: but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.

Sometimes evil becomes the occasion of good things, and God turns the crooked counsels of men to what is right. What I say will be made clearer by an example. Joseph's brothers, spurred on by the goads of their jealousy, sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty gold pieces (Gen. 37). This was the beginning of all good things for his father, for his brothers, and for all Egypt. Finally, he himself afterward said to his brothers: "You", he says, "thought evil things concerning me: and God thought good things concerning me" (Gen. 45:8). We can understand something similar in Onesimus too: evil beginnings were the occasions of a good thing. For if he had not run away from his master, he would never have come to Rome, where Paul was a prisoner in prison. If he had not seen Paul in chains, he would not have received faith in Christ. If he had not had the faith of Christ, he would never have been made Paul's son and sent into the work of the Gospel. From this, little by little and step by step, with the reasoning running back in reverse, Onesimus was made a minister of the Gospel precisely because he ran away from his master. But by adding perhaps he finely tempered his statement. For the judgments of God are hidden, and it is rash to pronounce as if on a certainty what is doubtful. Perhaps, he says, he therefore departed: cautiously, timidly, with trembling, and not with the whole foot firmly planted. For if he had not put perhaps, all slaves would have to run away in order to become apostolic men. As for his adding for an hour, we ought to take "hour" for "time". For in comparison with eternity, all time is short.
Commentary on Philemon

Onesimus, having offended his own master, fled on a long journey to the Apostle; to show that he did not depart for the purpose of being guilty of a crime, but so that, with sins forgiven, he might return useful to such an extent that he would not only become equal to his master in merits, but also a brother to the master himself. And so that Philemon may not suffer any disdain of pride, as is usual, as if the master were against the servant, he humbles himself when he calls him his brother both in the flesh and in the Lord; so that with the removal of the cause of human condition, because we are all descended from one Adam, we may recognize ourselves as brothers: especially when faith comes in the middle, which cuts off all pride.
Commentary on Philemon

So if you consider me as a partner, receive him as you would receive me. He shows such concern for Onesimus that he says Philemon, whom he praises above, should consider him as his own companion if he welcomes him as he would welcome an apostle. This is what Solomon said: A wise servant will have free people serving him (Eccles. 10:28). This saying is meant to scare Philemon, so that he may at least take him in for this reason if he cannot be swayed by love.
Homily on Philemon 3

No procedure is so apt to gain a hearing, as not to ask for everything at once. For see after how many praises, after how much preparation he hath introduced this great matter. After having said that he is "my son," that he is a partaker of the Gospel, that he is "my bowels," that thou receivest him back "as a brother," and "hold him as a brother," then he has added "as myself." And Paul was not ashamed to do this. For he who was not ashamed to be called the servant of the faithful, but confesses that he was such, much more would he not refuse this. But what he says is to this effect. If thou art of the same mind with me, if thou runnest upon the same terms, if thou considerest me a friend, receive him as myself.
Commentary on Philemon

If therefore you have me as a partner, receive him as me.

Philemon desired to have Paul as a partner, and, believing in Christ, he certainly wished to make such progress as to become like Paul and to share with him in his chains. Let us consider, therefore, how greatly Onesimus is praised here, and how far he is said to have progressed: for he is to be received as the Apostle is, and his master ought to desire his companionship just as he desires Paul's. In brief, what he says is this: If you wish to have me as a companion, have Onesimus too, whom I hold as my companion, and my son, and my bowels; if you do not receive him and are unwilling to have him, you yourself understand that you cannot have me.
Commentary on Philemon

If, however, something has hurt you, or he is a debtor, impute this to me. Now he undermines the excuse of anger, lest perhaps he would complain that he was hurt by him in such a way that it would not seem fitting to forgive him. But if it were so, he says it must be imputed to himself, through whom the heirs of the kingdom of heaven will be in the future, who have sinned before.
Homily on Philemon 3

"If he hath wronged thee at all." See where and when he has introduced the mention of the injury; last, after having said so many things in his behalf. For since the loss of money is particularly apt to annoy men, that he might not accuse him of this, (for it was most likely that it was spent,) then he brings in this, and says, "If he hath wronged thee." He does not say, If he has stolen anything; but what? "If he hath wronged thee." At the same time he both confessed the offense, and not as if it were the offense of a servant, but of a friend against a friend, making use of the expression of "wrong" rather than of theft.
Homily on Philemon 3

"Put that to mine account," he says, that is, reckon the debt to me, "I will repay it." Then also with that spiritual pleasantry, "I Paul write it with mine own hand." At once movingly and pleasantly; if when Paul did not refuse to execute a bond for him, he should refuse to receive him! This would both shame Philemon into compliance, and bring Onesimus out of trouble. "I write it," he says, "with mine own hand." Nothing is more affectionate than these "bowels," nothing more earnest, nothing more zealous. See what great concern he bestows in behalf of one man. "Albeit I do not say to thee how thou owest unto me even thine own self besides." Then that it might not appear insulting to him, whom he requests, if he had not the confidence to ask and obtain in behalf of a theft, he in some measure relieves this, saying, "That I say not unto thee how thou owest to me even thine own self besides." Not only thine own things, but thyself also. And this proceeded from love, and was according to the rule of friendship, and was a proof of his great confidence. See how he everywhere provides for both, that he may ask with great security, and that this may not seem a sign of too little confidence in him.
Commentary on Philemon

But if he has harmed you in anything, or owes you, charge this to me.

He imitates his Lord and has Christ speaking in him, so he ought to do, as far as his strength allows, the things that Christ does. For if He bore our infirmities and grieved over our wounds, the Apostle rightly puts himself forward on behalf of Onesimus and pledges to pay what Onesimus owed. But, as we said above, the whole of it is what was taken by theft and squandered in luxury and could not be repaid. Philemon weighed this against a great price: in return for a runaway slave and money lost, he would receive both a dearest brother and an eternal brother, and through him he would make the Apostle his debtor.
Commentary on Philemon

I Paul have written with my own hand. I will repay, not to say to you that you owe me even your own self.

What he says amounts to this: What Onesimus carried off by theft, I pledge that I will repay. Of this pledge this Epistle is witness, and so is my own hand, for I did not dictate it in the usual way but wrote it out myself with my own hand. Believe me, therefore, when I make a promise on behalf of Onesimus. But I say this as though speaking to a stranger. Otherwise, if I return to my own right: because of the word of Christ which I preached to you as the Gospel, and you were made a Christian, you owe me your own self. But if you are mine, then all that is yours is also mine: Onesimus too, who is yours, is mine. I could therefore have used him as my own; but I leave it to your will, so that you may have a reward by pardoning.
Homily on Philemon 3

What is, "Yea, brother"? Receive him, he says. For this we must understand though unexpressed. For dismissing all pleasantry, he again pursues his former considerations, that is, serious ones. And yet even these are serious. For the things that proceed from Saints are of themselves serious, even when they are pleasantry.
Homily on Philemon 3
"Yea, brother, let me have joy of thee in the Lord, refresh my heart in Christ." That is, thou grantest the favor to the Lord, not to me. "My heart," that is, toward thyself.
Commentary on Philemon

Yes, brother, may I enjoy you in the Lord.

The Latin tongue does not render the Greek idiom. For in what he says, ναὶ, ἀδελφέ, ναὶ is a kind of adverb, as it were, of one who speaks coaxingly. But we, in translating it yes (ita), brother, give out a sound that is somehow more watery and diluted, something rather other than what is written. For just as that Hebrew ANNA (אנה), for which the Seventy translators frequently rendered ὦ δή, signifies in its own language the feeling of one who entreats (whence Symmachus sometimes rendered ANNA as δέομαι, that is, "I beseech"), so we too suffer the same strain with the Greek language that the Greeks endure with the Hebrew. But what he says, may I enjoy you in the Lord, is understood as something far different from what is supposed. The Apostle enjoys no one except him who has in himself many virtues in harmony with one another, and all that Christ is called according to the variety of occasions: namely wisdom, justice, continence, gentleness, temperance, chastity. These he invokes upon Philemon, so that when he abounds in them, Paul himself, enjoying him to the full, may be filled. And lest you think that the enjoyment meant is that by which we often delight in one another's presence, he added, in the Lord: so that from the fact that the name of the Lord was joined to it, it might be understood that there is also another enjoyment, by which one may enjoy apart from the Lord.

Refresh my bowels in Christ. Just as he himself wishes to enjoy Philemon in the Lord, so he wishes his own bowels, Onesimus, whom he also called by the same name above, to be refreshed through Philemon. And it is said ambiguously: whether Onesimus is Paul's bowels in Christ, or whether Paul's bowels, Onesimus, are to be refreshed in Christ through Philemon. If you choose to take the former, Onesimus will rightly be called Paul's bowels in Christ, since Paul begot him for Christ in chains. If the latter, Onesimus is to be refreshed in Christ by Philemon, while he is instructed in Christ by Philemon's words.
On Christian Doctrine 1.33.37

But when you have joy of a man in God, it is God rather than man that you enjoy. For you enjoy Him by whom you are made happy, and you rejoice to have come to Him in whose presence you place your hope of joy. And accordingly, Paul says to Philemon, "Yea, brother, let me have joy of thee in the Lord." For if he had not added "in the Lord," but had only said, "Let me have joy of thee," he would have implied that he fixed his hope of happiness upon him, although even in the immediate context to "enjoy" is used in the sense of to "use with delight." For when the thing that we love is near us, it is a matter of course that it should bring delight with it. And if you pass beyond this delight, and make it a means to that which you are permanently to rest in, you are using it, and it is an abuse of language to say that you enjoy it. But if you cling to it, and rest in it, finding your happiness complete in it, then you may be truly and properly said to enjoy it. And this we must never do except in the case of the Blessed Trinity, who is the Supreme and Unchangeable Good.
Commentary on Philemon

Having confidence in your obedience, I have written to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say. I am now being affectionate, so that his obedience may be voluntary, in order to bear fruit. For by doing so, he provokes him to do more than is demanded of him; it often happens that when one sees themselves being thought highly of, they present themselves as even better.
Homily on Philemon 3

"Having confidence in thy obedience, I write unto thee." What stone would not these things have softened? What wild beast would not these things have rendered mild, and prepared to receive him heartily? After having borne witness to him by so many great testimonies of his goodness, he is not ashamed again to excuse himself. He says, Not barely requesting it, nor as commanding it, nor arbitrarily, but "having confidence in thy obedience I wrote unto thee." What he had said at the beginning, "having confidence," that he also says here in the sealing up of his letter.
Homily on Philemon 3

"Knowing that thou wilt also do more than I say." At the same time in saying this he excited him. For he would have been ashamed, though for nothing else, if having such credit with him as this, that he would do more than he said,-he should not do so much.
Commentary on Philemon

Confident of your obedience, I have written to you, knowing that you will do even beyond what I say.

He who presumes upon the one he is about to ask in some way forestalls him by that very presumption, so that he is not free to refuse what is asked. Moreover, if the one who makes the request knows that the person asked will do more than he asked, he asks for lesser things for this reason: so that the one asked may have a voluntary reward, and one made greater by what he performs. But if Philemon does these things at a man's command, how much more will he do them for the love of God? Hence he is deservedly praised by the voice of the Apostle, because he anticipates his commands in deed and can say: "Let the voluntary offerings of my mouth be pleasing to you, O Lord" (Ps. 118:108); and because, doing more than was commanded, he surpasses those who did only what they were ordered, and who are bidden to say: "We are unprofitable servants; what we ought to have done, we have done" (Luke 17:10). For this reason virginity too is crowned with a greater reward: it has no commandment of the Lord, and it reaches beyond what is commanded.
Commentary on Philemon

To make him more anxious and obedient, it is indicated that he will come; for those who are absent are usually despised. And the reason why the Apostle does not consider himself unworthy to be here yet, who has always suffered weariness and dangers, murders, persecutions, and chains, and whose rest was only in Christ alone? But for the progress of the believers, and to confound the enemies of the cross of Christ, he offered his own flesh to sufferings, in order to obtain crowns of immortality for his soul and body.
Homily on Philemon 3

"But withal prepare me also a lodging: for I trust that through your prayers I shall be given unto you." This also was the part of one who was exceedingly confident-or rather this too was in behalf of Onesimus, that not being indifferent, but knowing that he upon his return would know the things relating to him, they might lay aside all remembrance of the wrong, and might the rather grant the favor. For great was the influence and the honor of Paul residing among them, of Paul in his age, of Paul after imprisonment. Again, it is a proof of their love that he says that they pray; and to attribute to them so much as that they pray for "him." For although I be now in danger, yet nevertheless you will see me if ye pray for it.
Commentary on Philemon

At the same time, also prepare me a lodging.

I do not think the Apostle was so rich, or so encumbered with baggage, that he needed a lodging prepared for him. Nor do I think he was not content with a single little cell, he who would think a house small by the measure of his body most spacious. He says this rather so that, while Philemon expects him to come to him, he may all the more do what he has been asked. But if anyone thinks that this was commanded not by way of accommodation but in earnest, that a lodging should be prepared for him, then the lodging must be prepared for the apostle rather than for Paul. He was about to come to a new city, to preach the Crucified, and to bring doctrines never heard before, and he knew that very many would flock to him. It was therefore necessary, first, that the house be in a frequented part of the city, where people could easily gather. Next, that it be free of every disturbance; that it be ample, to hold a great many hearers; that it not be next to the places of the public shows; that it not be detestable for a shameful neighborhood; and lastly, that it be situated on the ground floor rather than in an upper room. For this reason I think that at Rome too he stayed two years in a rented house. Nor, I suppose, was the dwelling small to which crowds of Jews flocked daily.

For I hope that through your prayers I shall be given to you. God, when asked, grants a son to his father, and a brother is often saved by a brother's prayer. The Apostle, however, is granted at the prayers of the whole Church, for the benefit of those who are going to hear him. And this gift is said to be not so much toward him who, though prepared for martyrdom, is brought back from martyrdom, as toward those to whom the Apostle is sent. Paul himself says in another place that he was often in prison and was set free from chains: "In prisons frequently" (2 Cor. 11). He was released from these sometimes by the Lord's help, and frequently because the persecutors themselves found nothing in him worthy of death. For no decrees of the senate had yet been passed concerning the Christian name, and Nero's sword had not yet consecrated Christian blood. But because the preaching was new, the peoples were stirred to fury, either by the Jews out of envy or by those who saw their idols being destroyed. Then the preachers were sent to prison, and when the violence and fury had subsided they were let go again. The Acts of the Apostles testify that this is as we say, for there Felix too speaks to Agrippa: Paul could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar (Acts 25). Felix also says that he had found no charge except certain questions about their own religion and about a certain Jesus, whom Paul preached to be alive. From this we observe that they could likewise have been released by the other judges too, the Lord bringing this about so that the new preaching might be spread through the whole world.
Homily on Philemon 3

"Epaphras, my fellow-prisoner in Christ Jesus, saluteth thee." He was sent by the Colossians, so that from this it appears that Philemon was also at Colossae. And he calls him his "fellow-prisoner," showing that he also was in much tribulation, so that if not on his own account, yet on account of the other, it was right that he should be heard. For he that is in tribulation, and overlooks himself, and is concerned for others, deserves to be heard.
Homily on Philemon 3

And he puts him to shame from another consideration, if his countryman is a fellow-prisoner with Paul and suffers affliction with him, and he himself does not grant him a favor in behalf of his own servant. And he has added, "my fellow-prisoner in Christ Jesus," instead of on account of Christ.
The Apology of Rufinus, Book 1

There are one or two more things on which he wishes condemnation to be passed. One is this: that these men say that the body is a prison, and like a chain round the soul; and that they assert that the soul does not depart, but returns to the place where it originally was. Let me give quotations to show his opinion on this point also.... And in the Commentary on Paul's Epistle to Philemon, at the place where he says "Epaphras my fellow-prisoner greeteth you," some way down he says: "Possibly, however, as some think, a more recondite and mysterious view is set before us, namely, that the two companions had been captured and bound and brought down into this vale of tears." You see how he represents these opinions as things which are held as a kind of esoteric mystery by certain persons, of whom, however, he is one.
Commentary on Philemon

Epaphras my fellow captive in Christ Jesus greets you: Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, Luke, my fellow workers.

What we were saying at the beginning, that the Epistle to the Colossians was written at the same time and through the same bearer of the letters as the letter to Philemon, is also shown by the names of those who are introduced as sending greetings. For in that Epistle too it is written thus: "Aristarchus my fellow captive greets you, and Mark, the cousin of Barnabas, and Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ" (Col. 4:10, 12); and a little further on: "Luke the dearest physician greets you, and Demas; and say to Archippus: See the ministry which you have received in the Lord, that you fulfil it" (ibid. 14, 17); and: "Be mindful of my chains" (ibid. 18). But suppose someone thinks that they were not written together, because the Epistle to the Colossians has a few names that are not found written here. Let him know that not everyone is either a friend or an acquaintance of everyone, and that it is one thing for a private letter to be written to one man, and another for a public letter to be written to a whole church.
Commentary on Philemon

Epaphras my fellow captive in Christ Jesus greets you, he says. As to who Epaphras, Paul's fellow captive, may be, we have received the following story. They say that the parents of the Apostle Paul were from the district of Gischala in Judea. When the whole province was being laid waste by the Roman hand and the Jews were being scattered across the world, they were removed to Tarsus, a city of Cilicia, and the young Paul followed his parents' lot. In this way, they say, what he testifies of himself can stand: "They are Hebrews, so am I: they are Israelites, so am I: they are the seed of Abraham, so am I" (2 Cor. 11:22). And again elsewhere: "A Hebrew of Hebrews" (Phil. 3:5), and the other things which mark him as a Jew rather than a man of Tarsus. If this is so, we can suppose that Epaphras too was taken captive at the same time that Paul was taken, and that, having been settled with his parents at Colossae, a city of Asia, he afterwards received the word of Christ. Hence, as we said above, it is written to the Colossians: "Epaphras greets you, who is one of you, a servant of Christ, always anxious for you in prayers" (Col. 4:12). If this is the case, Aristarchus too, who in the same Epistle is called his fellow captive, will be brought to the same understanding. That holds unless perhaps something hidden and sacred, as some think, is shown in the word captivity: namely, that captured and bound alike, they were brought into this valley of tears. But if neither explanation is accepted, then from the fact that in Christ Jesus has been added here, we can suppose that he endured at Rome the same chains for Christ as Paul did, and that, just as he could be called a prisoner of Christ, so he could also be called His captive. Or at any rate it may be in this sense: that he too is noble among the apostles, like Andronicus and Julia, of whom it is written to the Romans: "Greet Andronicus and Julia, my kinsmen and my fellow captives, who are noble among the apostles, who also were in Christ Jesus before me" (Rom. 16:7). So much about Epaphras.
Commentary on Philemon

Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends greetings to you. Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers, also send their greetings. They all send their greetings and testify to their share in his glory.
Homily on Philemon 3

"Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, Luke, my fellow-workers." Why then does he put Luke last? And yet he elsewhere says, "Only Luke is with me" (2 Tim. iv. 11), and "Demas," he says, was one of those who "forsook him, having loved the present world." (2 Tim. iv. 10.) All these things, although they are mentioned elsewhere, yet nevertheless ought not to be passed over here without enquiry, nor ought we merely to hear them as things of course. But how comes he to say that he who forsook him salutes them? For "Erastus," he says, "abode at Corinth." (2 Tim. iv. 20.) He adds Epaphras, both as known to them, and being of their country. And Mark, as being himself also an admirable man. Why then does he number Demas with these? Perhaps it was after this that he became more remiss, when he saw the dangers multiplied. But Luke being last became first. And from these indeed he salutes him, urging him the more to obedience, and calls them his fellow-laborers, and in this way shames him into granting the request.
Commentary on Philemon

As for the rest, in writing the letter to Philemon he names as fellow workers in the Gospel and in his chains Mark, whom I take to be the writer of the Gospel; and Aristarchus, whom we mentioned above; and Demas, of whom he complains in another place: "Demas has forsaken me, loving the present world, and has gone to Thessalonica". And he names Luke the physician, who, in leaving the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles to the churches, was turned from a physician of bodies into a physician of souls, just as the apostles were made from fishers of fish into fishers of men (Matt. 4). Of him it is said in another place also: "I have sent", he says, "with him the brother whose praise is in the Gospel through all the churches" (2 Cor. 8:18). As often as his book is read in the churches, so often his medicine does not cease.
Commentary on Philemon
The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, amen. This is the subscription of the Apostle confirming the sent letter.
Homily on Philemon 3

"The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen."

He hath closed his Epistle with a prayer. And indeed prayer is a great good, salutary, and preservative of our souls. But it is great when we do things worthy of it, and do not render ourselves unworthy. And thou too, therefore, when thou goest to the priest, and he shall say to thee, "The Lord will have mercy on thee, my son," do not confide in the word only, but add also works. Do acts worthy of mercy, God will bless thee, my son, if indeed thou doest things worthy of blessing. He will bless thee, if thou showest mercy to thy neighbor. For the things which we wish to obtain from God, of those we ought first to impart to our neighbors. But if we deprive our neighbors of them, how can we wish to obtain them? "Blessed," He says, "are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy." For if men show mercy to such, much more will God, but to the unmerciful by no means. "For he shall have judgment without mercy to him that hath showed no mercy."
Commentary on Philemon

Grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.

Just as the people of Israel is numbered by the better part of man, the head, as Scripture says, according to their heads (Num. 1:2), so the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ is indeed in the whole man and in every part of the saints. But by synecdoche it is said of the whole man, from the greater and better part, that is, the spirit: Grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. And when grace is in the spirit, it makes the whole man spiritual, so that the flesh too serves the spirit, and the soul is not overcome by the flesh, and, brought together into a spiritual substance, cleaves to the Lord; for he who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit (1 Cor. 6).

intro: . < Previous Chapter ----- Next Chapter > THE EPISTLE OF ST. PAUL, THE APOSTLE, TO PHILEMON. PREFACE. Philemon was a rich man, of high birth. He had been converted by St. Paul, when he was preaching at Ephesus, or by his disciple Epaphras. His house was become not unlike a church. Onesimus, his slave, far from profiting by the excellent example set before him, became more wicked; he plundered his master, and flew to Rome, where St. Paul was detained in prison for the first time. He received the poor fugitive charitably, and wrote to his master in his behalf. --- The letter seems to have been written in the year sixty-one[A.D. 61], during St. Paul's first imprisonment at Rome. It contains, as St. Chrysostom observes, divers profitable instructions, and marks of St. Paul's charity towards a poor fugitive servant. Erasmus says Cicero never wrote with greater eloquence. (Witham)
